title: Fluent adding and subtracting within 20
keyIdea: Fluent within 20 means you know from memory every sum of two one-digit numbers, and the related take-aways, using doubles and near-doubles as anchors — without recounting every counter each time.
familyTip: Fire a quick round: 8+8, 7+8, 9+6, 16−7. Celebrate snap answers. If your child counts every finger, pause and ask: what double is close?

visual.caption: Fluent fact or recount trap? Drag each into its box, or tap then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: doubles wall, near-doubles, snap recall, related take-aways, catch recount myth.

kid: Fluent within 20 means you know the answer straight away for sums like 8+8 or 9+6.
A double is a number plus itself: 6+6=12, 7+7=14, 8+8=16, 9+9=18. These are anchor facts.
A near-double is one more than a double. 7+8 is double 7, then plus 1, which is 15.
If you know 9+7=16, you also know 16−7=9. Related facts share the same three numbers.
adult: Ages 7 to 8. CCSS 2.OA.2: fluently add and subtract within 20 using mental strategies; by end of Grade 2, know from memory all sums of two one-digit numbers. Builds on addition and subtraction within 20 (strategies) and fluent within 10.

Doubles and near-doubles are the main memory anchors. Make-ten is still a strategy (taught in the within-20 strategies lesson); this lesson pushes the known-from-memory bar for one-digit + one-digit and related subtraction.
Common mistakes: sticking digits together (9+6 as 96); always recounting every counter; treating fluency as only make-10 pairs; and forgetting that related subtraction uses the same three numbers.
In the lab your child builds doubles, opens a near-double for 7+8, snaps 9+6, derives 16−7 from 9+7, and rejects the 'always recount' myth.

practice.hint: A double is a number added to itself. Twice eight.
practice.explain: 8 + 8 is the double of 8, which is 16. Not eighty-eight.

practice.hint: Double 7 is 14. Near-double means add one more.
practice.explain: Double 7 is 14. 7 + 8 is one more than that double, so 15.

practice.hint: This is a double. The same number plus itself.
Related facts share the same three numbers: 9, 7 and 16.
practice.explain: If 9 + 7 = 16, then 16 − 7 = 9. Keep the same three numbers.

practice.hint: Double {a}, then add one for the near-double.
practice.explain: Double {a} is {=a+a}. Plus one more is {=a+a+1}.

pool.hint: Snap the one-digit sum. Do not stick the digits together.
pool.explain: 9 + 6 = 15. Sticking digits would wrongly make ninety-six.

pool.hint: Fluency is quick known facts, not endless recounting.
pool.explain: By the end of this stage you know every sum of two one-digit numbers from memory.

pool.hint: A double take-away one of the parts leaves the other part.

pool.prompt: Which is a within-20 one-digit sum?
pool.explain: 9 and 8 are one-digit; 17 is within 20. The others use a two-digit addend or go past.

pool.prompt: A mix-up says 9 + 6 = 96. What went wrong?
pool.hint: Joining digit glyphs is not adding their values.
pool.explain: Sticking 9 and 6 makes ninety-six. Adding values makes fifteen.

pool.hint: Near-double: twice the number, plus one.

choices: They are known anchors for near-doubles
pool.hint: Near-doubles sit one away from a known double.
pool.explain: Knowing 7+7 unlocks 7+8. Doubles are memory anchors, not the only facts.
